topics.title: Starting homework
topics.desc: Pick one assignment. Open it and write down the smallest thing you can do next, such as reading the first question. Set a five-minute timer and do just that step. When it rings, decide on the next one.

topics.title: Remembering what you study
topics.desc: Close your notes and try answering a question from memory. Check your answer, then try the ones you missed again tomorrow. For vocabulary, practice in both directions: word to meaning and meaning to word.

topics.title: Writing a paragraph
topics.desc: Write your main point in one sentence. Add one detail or quote that supports it, then explain how that detail proves your point. Read the sentences together and check that each one helps explain the same idea.

topics.title: Planning your day
topics.desc: Start with commitments that already have a time. Pick the one remaining task that matters most and give it a time slot. Leave a little space between tasks in case one takes longer.

topics.title: Ideas for boredom
topics.desc: Try a ten-minute challenge: photograph three ordinary objects so they look unusual, draw a map of a made-up place, or invent a game using only paper and a coin.

topics.title: How rain forms
topics.desc: Water evaporates from surfaces and enters the air as vapor. When moist air cools, some vapor condenses into cloud droplets. Droplets can join and grow heavy enough to fall as rain.

topics.title: Why the sky looks blue
topics.desc: Sunlight contains many colors. Air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths, including blue, more strongly than longer wavelengths like red. That scattered light reaches your eyes from all across the sky.

topics.title: Changing seasons
topics.desc: Earth's axis is tilted. When your hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight hits it more directly and the days are longer. Six months later, the other hemisphere tilts toward the Sun.

topics.title: Moon phases
topics.desc: The Sun lights roughly half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that sunlit half. A crescent means only a narrow slice of the lit side faces us.

topics.title: Percent of a number
topics.desc: Percent means out of 100. To find a percentage of a number, divide the percentage by 100 and multiply by the number. For example, 15 percent of 80 is 0.15 times 80, which is 12.

topics.title: Sale prices
topics.desc: For a 20% discount, you pay 80% of the original price. Multiply the original price by 0.80. For example, a $30 item costs $24 before tax.

topics.title: Finding an average
topics.desc: Add the values together and divide by how many values there are. For 6, 8 and 10, the sum is 24. There are three values, so the average is 8.

topics.title: Wi-Fi and Ethernet
topics.desc: Wi-Fi sends data by radio between your device and router. Ethernet uses a cable. For gaming, Ethernet often gives more consistent timing because nearby wireless traffic and walls do not affect the cable.

topics.title: What localhost means
topics.desc: Localhost points back to the device opening the link. If a friend opens your localhost address, their browser looks on their own device. A published website gives both of you a link to the same hosted files.

topics.title: Storage and memory
topics.desc: Storage keeps files after an app closes. RAM holds the data an app is currently using. When you open a website, the browser uses RAM and may save files in its cache so the page loads faster next time.

topics.title: Making a sandwich
topics.desc: Try bread, a spread you like, and a filling such as cheese or sliced vegetables. For a packed lunch, dry damp vegetables and keep juicy ingredients separate until you eat.

topics.title: Finding a lost item
topics.desc: Think of the last moment you remember using it. Walk that route slowly, checking surfaces where you put things down. Then check pockets, bags and the gaps beside furniture one area at a time.

topics.title: Apologizing to a friend
topics.desc: Name what you did, acknowledge how it affected them and say what you'll do differently. For example: “I interrupted you in front of everyone. That was unfair. Next time I'll let you finish.”

topics.title: Greetings
topics.desc: Hey! You can ask me about everyday things like planning homework, making lunch, Wi-Fi or why the sky is blue. The topic menu shows everything I've learned.

topics.title: Variables
topics.desc: A variable is a name that refers to a value. Assignment uses one equals sign. You can use the old value when calculating the new one.

topics.title: Printing
topics.desc: Use print() to display values. Put text in quotes. You can pass several values separated by commas.

topics.title: User input
topics.desc: input() shows a prompt and returns the user's reply as text. For this example, suppose the user types Ada.

topics.title: Converting types
topics.desc: Use int() for whole numbers, float() for decimals, and str() for text. The text you convert must have a valid format for that conversion.

topics.title: Strings
topics.desc: A string holds text. A slice like [1:4] takes characters at positions 1, 2 and 3. Counting starts at zero. upper() returns uppercase text.

topics.title: Lists
topics.desc: A list holds items in order. Index 0 selects the first item. Index -1 selects the last one.

topics.title: Appending items
topics.desc: Use append() to add one item to the end of an existing list. It changes the list in place.

topics.title: For loops
topics.desc: A for loop takes one item at a time from a sequence. Indent every line you want to run for each item.

topics.title: While loops
topics.desc: A while loop checks its condition before each pass. Here, adding one eventually makes the condition false.

topics.title: Range
topics.desc: range(start, stop, step) produces integers up to the stop value, excluding it. With one argument, counting starts at zero.

topics.title: Conditionals
topics.desc: An if statement checks a condition. elif checks another condition if earlier checks failed. else handles the remaining cases.

topics.title: Equality
topics.desc: Use == to test whether two values are equal. Use = to assign a value to a name.

topics.title: Functions
topics.desc: Use def to define a function. Parameters receive values when you call it. A return statement sends a result back to the caller.

topics.title: Return values
topics.desc: return ends a function call and passes a value back. print() displays a value. A function that reaches its end without returning a value gives the caller None.
topics.code:
def total(a, b):
    return a + b
answer = total(4, 5)
print(answer)

topics.title: Dictionaries
topics.desc: A dictionary maps keys to values. Use square brackets for a known key. Use get() with a default for a key that might be missing.

topics.title: Indentation
topics.desc: Indentation groups lines into blocks. After a line such as if ready:, indent the lines that belong inside it. Four spaces per level is the usual style.
topics.code:
ready = True
if ready:
    print("Start")
print("Done")

topics.title: Index errors
topics.desc: IndexError means the requested position is outside the sequence. A list with three items has nonnegative indices 0, 1 and 2.

topics.title: Name errors
topics.desc: NameError means Python could not find a name. Check spelling, capitalization and whether the assignment ran before the name was used.

topics.title: Soccer first touch
topics.desc: Let the ball meet the inside of your foot and draw your foot back slightly. Aim your first touch into space where you can take the next step.

topics.title: Passing in soccer
topics.desc: Plant your standing foot beside the ball, point it toward your target and use the inside of your other foot. Practice against a wall with a small target.

topics.title: Checking your shoulder
topics.desc: Glance over your shoulder before the pass arrives. Look for a teammate, a defender and a patch of space, then bring your eyes back to the ball.

topics.title: Packing for practice
topics.desc: Lay out your footwear, shin guards, socks, water bottle and the kit your coach requested. Pack a spare shirt for the trip home.

topics.title: Comparing game settings
topics.desc: Change one setting at a time. Repeat the same short drill at each setting and record accuracy and comfort before deciding.

topics.title: Frame rate
topics.desc: FPS counts how many frames a game produces per second. At 60 FPS an evenly spaced frame takes about 16.7 milliseconds. Uneven timing can still look choppy.

topics.title: Refresh rate
topics.desc: Hertz tells you how many times per second a display can refresh. A 120 Hz display can refresh 120 times each second; the game also has to supply frames.

topics.title: Game latency
topics.desc: Ping usually measures a network round trip in milliseconds. A 30 ms result means the trip there and back took about 30 milliseconds. Spikes can matter as much as the average.

topics.title: Bandwidth
topics.desc: Bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry per second. Eight megabits make one megabyte, so 80 Mbps is at most about 10 MB per second before overhead.

topics.title: Screen resolution
topics.desc: Resolution gives the number of pixels across and down. A 2560 by 1440 image contains 3,686,400 pixels. Screen size determines how spread out they look.

topics.title: Bookmarks
topics.desc: A bookmark saves the address of a page. Use the browser’s bookmark or favorites command, give it a recognizable name, and open it later from your bookmarks.

topics.title: ZIP files
topics.desc: A ZIP archive bundles files together and can compress them. Extract it to get ordinary files you can open or edit individually.

topics.title: File extensions
topics.desc: An extension is the ending after a filename’s final dot. It often identifies the format: .txt for plain text, .html for a webpage and .jpg for a JPEG image. Renaming the ending alone does not convert the contents.

topics.title: Saving versions
topics.desc: Save a working version before a major change. With Git, commit a small set of related edits and describe what changed so you can find that version later.

topics.title: What a repository is
topics.desc: A repository holds a project’s files and change history. A README explains how to use the project. Commits mark changes you can inspect later.

topics.title: Static websites
topics.desc: A static host sends files such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The browser can still run interactive code, like a quiz or a small model, after those files arrive.

topics.title: HTML and CSS
topics.desc: HTML gives a page its structure, such as headings and buttons. CSS controls appearance and layout. JavaScript can add behavior when you press a button.

topics.title: Debugging
topics.desc: Try the smallest input that triggers the problem. Write down what you expected, then check the actual values one step at a time until they diverge.

topics.title: Pseudocode
topics.desc: Write the steps without worrying about syntax. For a score counter: start at zero, read each result, add one for a win, then display the total.

topics.title: Testing software
topics.desc: Choose an input and write the expected result before running it. Try a typical case, an empty input and a boundary case. If you fix a bug, rerun the input that exposed it.

topics.title: Learning from examples
topics.desc: During training a model makes a prediction, measures the error and adjusts numbers called weights. Separate practice examples from test examples to check whether it learned patterns that generalize.

topics.title: Generating text
topics.desc: A language model estimates which piece of text might come next. It picks one, adds it to the context and repeats. This can produce a sentence the model never saw as a whole.

topics.title: Overfitting
topics.desc: A model can learn details that work only on its training set. Test it on independently written examples. A large training-to-test performance gap is one clue to investigate.

topics.title: Game practice routines
topics.desc: Choose one skill, such as tracking a moving target. Do a short repeatable drill, play one round focusing on it, and note one thing to change next time.

topics.title: Creative game ideas
topics.desc: Pick one action, one obstacle and one win condition. For example: steer a bouncing ball, dodge moving gates and reach three checkpoints. Prototype that before adding more features.

topics.title: MVPs
topics.desc: Choose one person, one problem and one working feature. For a homework planner, a list with due dates might be enough to test whether someone actually uses it.

topics.title: Customer interviews
topics.desc: Ask about the last time the problem happened. What did they do, how long did it take and what was frustrating? Concrete stories tell you more than asking whether an idea sounds cool.

topics.title: Project pitches
topics.desc: Describe who it helps, the problem and what the person can do with it. End with a short example or demonstration.

topics.title: Naming a project
topics.desc: List words describing the goal and the audience. Pair two, say each candidate aloud and see whether someone can spell it after hearing it once.

topics.title: Feedback
topics.desc: Point to one specific detail, say what effect it had, then suggest one change. For example: the button label helped me start, but I couldn't find the back button.

topics.title: Group projects
topics.desc: List the deliverables, give each one an owner and agree on a check-in before the deadline. Leave time for everyone to review the combined result.

topics.title: Summarizing
topics.desc: Name the main idea in one sentence. Add only the details needed to understand it. Check that the summary keeps the author’s meaning and uses your own wording.

topics.title: Quoting evidence
topics.desc: Introduce who is speaking, copy the relevant words exactly and give the citation your teacher requested. Follow it with your explanation of how the quote supports your point.

topics.title: Proofreading
topics.desc: Read once for meaning, once for sentence boundaries and once for spelling. Reading aloud slowly can reveal a missing word your eyes skipped.

topics.title: Note taking
topics.desc: Use a short heading for each idea. Write a key point in your own words, add one example, and mark anything you need to ask about later.

topics.title: Giving a presentation
topics.desc: Build the talk around one message. Use slides to show a useful example or image, and rehearse aloud with a timer. Practice the opening and closing separately.

topics.title: Emailing a teacher
topics.desc: Use a subject that names the assignment. In the message, explain what you tried, ask one specific question, then sign your name.

topics.title: Fractions
topics.desc: Use a common denominator before adding. For example, one half plus one third becomes three sixths plus two sixths, which equals five sixths.

topics.title: Ratios
topics.desc: A ratio compares amounts in order. Two red beads for every three blue beads scales to four red and six blue when you double both amounts.

topics.title: Rectangle area
topics.desc: Multiply length by width using the same unit for both. A rectangle 4 cm by 7 cm covers 28 square centimeters.

topics.title: Circle area
topics.desc: Multiply pi by the radius squared. For radius 3 cm, the area is 9 pi square centimeters, about 28.27 square centimeters.

topics.title: Perimeter
topics.desc: Add the lengths of all outer sides. A rectangle 4 meters by 7 meters has perimeter 4 + 7 + 4 + 7 = 22 meters.

topics.title: Unit conversions
topics.desc: One meter equals 100 centimeters. Multiply meters by 100 to get centimeters. Divide centimeters by 100 to get meters.

topics.title: Reading graphs
topics.desc: Read the title and axis labels first. Check what one tick means and whether the scale starts at zero. Then compare the values the graph actually shows.

topics.title: Elapsed time
topics.desc: Count forward in easy jumps. From 3:45 to 5:10, count 15 minutes to 4:00, one hour to 5:00 and ten minutes more: 1 hour 25 minutes.

topics.title: Probability
topics.desc: When outcomes are equally likely, divide the number of favorable outcomes by the total number. Rolling an even number on a fair six-sided die has probability three sixths, or one half.

topics.title: Shadows
topics.desc: A shadow forms when an object blocks light. When the Sun is low in the sky, its rays hit the ground at a shallow angle and a standing object's shadow stretches farther.

topics.title: Echoes
topics.desc: Sound travels to a surface and reflects. If the reflected sound reaches you late enough to hear it separately, you hear an echo.

topics.title: Condensation
topics.desc: Water vapor in the surrounding air cools against the cold glass. Some turns into liquid droplets on the outside.

topics.title: Evaporation
topics.desc: Some water molecules at the surface escape into the air. Moving air helps wet clothes dry by carrying away humid air near the fabric.

topics.title: Floating
topics.desc: Water pushes upward on an object. A floating boat displaces enough water for that upward force to balance its weight. Its hollow shape helps it displace a lot of water.

topics.title: Day and night
topics.desc: Earth rotates. Your location turns toward the Sun for daylight and away from it for night. This rotation makes the Sun appear to move across the sky.

topics.title: Stars twinkling
topics.desc: Starlight passes through moving layers of air with different temperatures. These layers bend the light by changing amounts, making a distant star appear to flicker.

topics.title: Rhythm practice
topics.desc: Set a slow, comfortable beat and tap once per click. Count groups of four aloud. Speed up only when the beat feels even.

topics.title: Photo composition
topics.desc: Imagine a three-by-three grid. Try placing the subject near a grid intersection, check the edges for distractions, then try a centered shot and compare the two.

topics.title: Steady video
topics.desc: Hold the phone with two hands, keep your elbows close and start recording before the action. For a still shot, rest the phone on a stable surface.

topics.title: Story structure
topics.desc: Give a character a goal, put a specific obstacle in the way and let a choice change what happens. End by showing a consequence of that choice.

topics.title: Packing a bag
topics.desc: Check tomorrow’s schedule. Pack the books and materials you actually need, place completed work in one folder, and keep frequently used items in an accessible pocket.

topics.title: Tidying a desk
topics.desc: Clear one section. Put items you use daily within reach, gather loose papers in one place and give everything else a home before moving to the next section.

topics.title: Shopping lists
topics.desc: Check what you already have, write down what is missing and group it by store section. Put quantities beside anything where the amount matters.

topics.title: Following a recipe
topics.desc: Read the full recipe first. Gather the ingredients and tools, check the amounts and lay out ingredients in the order you will use them.

topics.title: Making plans with a friend
topics.desc: Suggest one activity and a specific time. Make it easy to offer another option: “Want to play on Saturday afternoon? Sunday works for me too.”

topics.title: Choosing between options
topics.desc: Choose two or three criteria you care about and compare each option against the same criteria. If the decision is reversible, a small trial can answer more than guessing.

topics.title: PlayStation 5
topics.desc: PS5 stands for PlayStation 5. It is Sony’s home video game console. You connect it to a TV or monitor and use a controller to play games.

topics.title: Xbox
topics.desc: Xbox is Microsoft’s gaming brand. An Xbox console, such as an Xbox Series X or Series S, is a device you connect to a screen to play video games.

topics.title: Nintendo Switch
topics.desc: Nintendo Switch is a family of video game consoles from Nintendo. The original Switch can be played as a handheld or connected to a TV through its dock. The Switch Lite is handheld only.

topics.title: Graphics processors
topics.desc: A GPU is a graphics processing unit. It performs many calculations in parallel, which helps produce the images in a game. A graphics card is hardware that contains a GPU.

topics.title: Central processors
topics.desc: A CPU is a central processing unit. It runs program instructions, such as calculating a score or deciding which part of an app to run next.

topics.title: Bluetooth
topics.desc: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology that lets devices exchange data. Pairing introduces two devices so they can connect, such as a phone and a pair of headphones.

topics.title: BMX
topics.desc: BMX stands for bicycle motocross. BMX includes racing on tracks and freestyle riding. BMX bikes are typically compact and built for the type of riding they are used for.

topics.title: HDMI
topics.desc: HDMI stands for High-Definition Multimedia Interface. An HDMI cable can carry digital video and audio from a console or computer to a compatible display.

topics.title: Sorting laundry
topics.desc: Separate new dark or bright items from whites. Group the rest by care instructions and fabric weight so rough towels don't rub delicate shirts.

topics.title: Laundry symbols
topics.desc: The tub is washing, triangle is bleach, square is drying and iron is ironing. A crossed-out symbol rules out that process; dots usually indicate heat level.

topics.title: Turning clothes inside out
topics.desc: Turning a printed shirt inside out reduces rubbing against the drum and other clothes. Follow the label for temperature and drying.

topics.title: Air-drying clothes
topics.desc: Lay heavy wet knits flat in their original shape. For lighter shirts, smooth the seams and spread the weight across a rack.

topics.title: Folding a fitted sheet
topics.desc: Tuck one elastic corner into the next until they nest. Lay the sheet flat, fold the curved edges inward and fold the resulting rectangle.

topics.title: How a PS5 runs a game
topics.desc: When you press jump, the controller sends an input. The game uses the CPU to check the rules and update your character's position. The GPU draws the next view, and HDMI carries it to your screen. The SSD supplies game data and RAM holds what the processors need right now.

topics.title: Charging speed
topics.desc: Charging speed depends on the power source, cable and device together. Two cables with identical plugs can support different power levels. The device can also slow charging as its battery fills.

topics.title: Untying a shoelace knot
topics.desc: Push some slack toward the knot from both sides, then roll the knot between your fingers. Pull a loosened loop outward before pulling the ends apart.

topics.title: Tying shoelaces
topics.desc: Cross the laces once, make a loop, wrap the other lace around it and push a second loop through. Tighten by pulling the loops sideways.

topics.title: Packing shoes
topics.desc: Brush loose dirt off and put shoes in a separate washable bag. Pack them near the edges and fill the empty space inside with small items.

topics.title: Measuring inseam
topics.desc: Lay a well-fitting pair flat. Measure along the inside seam from where the legs meet down to the hem.

topics.title: Reading a size chart
topics.desc: Compare the chart's specific measurements to yours. Check whether it lists body or garment measurements. Compare a similar garment you own if the chart lists garment dimensions.

topics.title: Removing lint
topics.desc: Make light passes with a lint roller or clothing brush. Check fabric care instructions before treating stubborn pills.

topics.title: Making a bed
topics.desc: Match the long edges of the fitted sheet to the long edges of the mattress. Seat opposite corners in turn. If it repeatedly slips, check the sheet's pocket depth.

topics.title: Game update storage
topics.desc: An update may keep the old files while downloading or rebuilding new ones. The temporary free space requested can exceed the final increase in installed size.

topics.title: Hanging a poster
topics.desc: Check which removable mounting product suits the surface and poster weight. Clean and dry the spot first, and follow the product's removal instructions.

topics.title: Organizing cables
topics.desc: Trace each cable from device to plug, label its ends and bundle cables going the same way with reusable ties. Leave slack for moving the device.

topics.title: Labeling boxes
topics.desc: Mark the room and two or three specific contents on two visible sides. Mark things you need first so they can stay accessible.

topics.title: Sorting papers
topics.desc: Make three piles: action needed, keep for reference and recycle. File by class and keep current assignments together at the front.

topics.title: Sweeping a floor
topics.desc: Keep the dustpan lip flat and brush toward it with short strokes. Shift the pan back slightly to pick up the final line.

topics.title: Wiping a mirror
topics.desc: Use a clean microfiber cloth with a small amount of suitable glass cleaner. Follow with a dry section before streaks set.

topics.title: Handwashing dishes
topics.desc: Remove food first and wash in warm soapy water. Start with less greasy items, change dirty water and rinse off the soap.

topics.title: Loading a dishwasher
topics.desc: Face dirty surfaces toward the spray and leave gaps between items. Spin the spray arm by hand before starting to check clearance.

topics.title: Keeping a chore chart
topics.desc: List each job, its owner and when it is due. Put a visible check beside completed tasks and rotate shared jobs on a regular schedule.

topics.title: Reusing cardboard
topics.desc: Cut and fold scrap cardboard into a rough model of the object you want to build. Test shape and size before spending time on stronger materials.

topics.title: Measuring flour
topics.desc: If a recipe gives grams, weigh the flour. For cup measurements, loosen the flour, spoon it into the cup and level it without packing it down.

topics.title: Measuring liquids
topics.desc: Set the measuring cup on a level surface. Bring your eyes level with the mark and read the bottom of the curve for water.

topics.title: Teaspoons and tablespoons
topics.desc: One US tablespoon equals three US teaspoons. Half a tablespoon is one and a half teaspoons.

topics.title: Scaling a recipe
topics.desc: Multiply each ingredient quantity by the same factor. Pan depth and cooking time can change differently, so check the recipe's doneness cues.

topics.title: Making a vinaigrette
topics.desc: Whisk vinegar and seasoning, then add oil gradually while whisking. Oil and vinegar separate over time; shake or whisk again before serving.

topics.title: Layering a yogurt parfait
topics.desc: Layer yogurt and fruit, then add granola just before eating if you want crunch. Pack the granola separately when taking it along.

topics.title: Building a wrap
topics.desc: Use less filling and leave a border. Fold the sides over the filling, bring the near edge up and roll while keeping the sides tucked.

topics.title: Packing crunchy snacks
topics.desc: Use a rigid reusable container with a lid. Pack it above heavy items and keep wet ingredients separate.

topics.title: Peeling an orange
topics.desc: Start at the loose end with your thumb and peel in sections, sliding your finger under the rind instead of pressing into the fruit.

topics.title: Picking a ripe banana
topics.desc: Green bananas are firmer and less sweet. Yellow fruit with a few brown speckles is usually softer and sweeter; prefer the stage that fits the recipe.

topics.title: Keeping guacamole green
topics.desc: Cutting exposes enzymes and other compounds to oxygen, which produces brown pigments. Limit air contact and refrigerate the covered avocado; citrus juice can slow browning.

topics.title: Washing produce
topics.desc: Wash produce under running water and rub its surface gently. Use a clean produce brush for firm skins. Skip soap on food.

topics.title: Draining pasta
topics.desc: A colander lets water pass through while holding the pasta. If the recipe uses cooking water for sauce, reserve some before draining.

topics.title: Pasta shapes
topics.desc: Ridged or hollow shapes catch chunky sauces, while long strands work well with smoother sauces. The shape changes how much sauce comes with each bite.

topics.title: Fluffing rice
topics.desc: After resting the cooked rice as directed, lift and separate the grains gently with a fork. Stirring hard can crush the grains.

topics.title: Mixing batter
topics.desc: Slide a spatula down the side, sweep across the bottom and lift batter over the top. Turn the bowl and repeat gently to keep trapped air.

topics.title: Proofing dough
topics.desc: Yeast releases carbon dioxide as it uses sugars. The dough traps some of that gas, causing it to expand before baking.

topics.title: Preheating an oven
topics.desc: Preheating brings the oven near the recipe's starting temperature. Starting cold changes how quickly dough rises, spreads or sets.

topics.title: Lining a baking sheet
topics.desc: Baking parchment gives food a release surface and makes cleanup easier. Check its temperature limit and use the liner specified by the recipe.

topics.title: Softening butter
topics.desc: Softened butter dents when pressed but keeps its shape. Melted butter behaves differently when mixed with sugar, which can change how cookies spread.

topics.title: Seasoning gradually
topics.desc: Add a small amount, stir and taste before adding more when the dish is safe to taste. You can add seasoning more easily than remove it.

topics.title: Reading an ingredient list
topics.desc: On most US packaged foods, ingredients appear in descending order by weight at the time of formulation. The first usually contributes the most weight.

topics.title: Meal planning
topics.desc: Choose two or three meals that share ingredients, then vary the preparation. Bread, vegetables and cheese might cover sandwiches one day and toast with toppings another.

topics.title: Organizing a pantry
topics.desc: Group similar items together, put newer purchases behind older ones and keep labels visible. Check dates when planning meals.

topics.title: Writing a recipe card
topics.desc: Write the ingredients with quantities, serving yield, equipment and steps in order. Record changes that worked so you can repeat them.

topics.title: Finding a thesis
topics.desc: Ask which idea the writer wants you to accept. Find the sentence the examples consistently support; it often appears near the beginning but may be implied.

topics.title: Writing a thesis
topics.desc: Turn a broad subject into a claim someone could discuss. Instead of “public parks,” try “The town should keep its park open later because students need space after practice.”

topics.title: Topic versus theme
topics.desc: A topic can be one word, such as loyalty. A theme says something about that topic, such as “loyalty sometimes requires an uncomfortable choice.”

topics.title: First-person narration
topics.desc: A first-person narrator participates in or witnesses events and uses words like I and we. Look at the narration outside quoted dialogue.

topics.title: Third-person narration
topics.desc: In third person the narrator describes characters from outside using names, he, she or they. Whose thoughts the narrator reveals tells you more about the viewpoint.

topics.title: Making an inference
topics.desc: Combine a specific clue with what you know, then check your inference against the rest of the passage. A slammed door may suggest anger, depending on the context.

topics.title: Context clues
topics.desc: Read the sentences around the word for examples, contrasts or definitions. Substitute your guessed meaning and see whether the passage still makes sense.

topics.title: Fact versus opinion
topics.desc: A factual claim can be checked against evidence even if it turns out false. An opinion expresses a judgment, preference or evaluation.

topics.title: Cause and effect
topics.desc: Find the event or action and then what changed because of it. Words like because and therefore help, but two events in sequence do not automatically have a causal link.

topics.title: Compare and contrast
topics.desc: Choose one comparison point at a time. Give evidence for each character on that same point before moving to the next.

topics.title: Transitions
topics.desc: Name the relationship between the ideas first. Use a phrase like “for example,” “in contrast” or “as a result” only if it fits that relationship.

topics.title: Paraphrasing
topics.desc: Read until you understand it, set it aside and explain the idea from memory. Check accuracy and cite the source when using its ideas.

topics.title: Using an index
topics.desc: Look up the term alphabetically in the index at the back. Follow the listed page numbers and try a related term if the first one is missing.

topics.title: Using a glossary
topics.desc: Check the glossary, usually near the back, for short definitions used by that book. An index instead tells you where a term appears.

topics.title: Bibliographies
topics.desc: Save the author, title, publisher or site, date, URL and page number when applicable. Format them later according to the style the assignment requires.

topics.title: Primary sources
topics.desc: A primary source provides direct evidence for the question you are studying, such as a diary from the event, raw observations or a photograph.

topics.title: Secondary sources
topics.desc: A secondary source interprets or analyzes other evidence. A later historian's account typically serves this role when studying an earlier event.

topics.title: Reading a rubric
topics.desc: Turn each criterion into something you can find in your draft. Compare that evidence to the description of your target performance level.

topics.title: Checking assignment directions
topics.desc: Underline action words like compare or explain. List the required product, evidence, format and due date; ask about any missing detail.

topics.title: Spelling practice
topics.desc: Identify the exact letter pattern you miss, write it correctly once, cover it and try from memory. Check again after a short break.

topics.title: Subject-verb agreement
topics.desc: Find the subject before choosing the verb. “The box of pencils is missing” uses is because box is singular.

topics.title: Apostrophes
topics.desc: For most singular nouns, add apostrophe-s: the player's bag. For a regular plural ending in s, add the apostrophe after it: the players' bags.

topics.title: Run-on sentences
topics.desc: Separate two complete clauses with a period, or join them with a comma and a coordinating conjunction such as but. A comma alone often creates a comma splice.

topics.title: Dialogue punctuation
topics.desc: In US English, enclose spoken words in quotation marks. For example: Maya said, “I found it.” Start a new paragraph when the speaker changes.

topics.title: Peer editing
topics.desc: Read for the main claim first. Point out one place that works and one place where you needed more explanation, using a specific sentence as evidence.

topics.title: Place value
topics.desc: Each position to the right is one tenth of the previous position. In 3.47 the 4 represents four tenths and the 7 represents seven hundredths.

topics.title: Rounding
topics.desc: Find the tenths digit, then inspect the hundredths digit. Using the usual school rule, 4.76 rounds to 4.8 because the next digit is 6.

topics.title: Comparing decimals
topics.desc: Line up the decimal points and append trailing zeros. Compare from the left: 0.50 exceeds 0.40 because five tenths exceeds four tenths.

topics.title: Multiplying decimals
topics.desc: Multiply as whole numbers and put back as many decimal places as the factors have together. For example, 1.2 times 0.3 equals 0.36.

topics.title: Dividing decimals
topics.desc: Multiply both numbers by the same power of ten until the divisor becomes a whole number. For example, 4.8 divided by 0.6 becomes 48 divided by 6.

topics.title: Negative numbers
topics.desc: Farther right on a number line means greater. Minus three is to the right of minus eight and is closer to zero.

topics.title: Absolute value
topics.desc: Absolute value measures distance from zero, so both −7 and 7 have absolute value 7.

topics.title: Order of operations
topics.desc: Evaluate grouping first, then exponents, then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right.

topics.title: Exponents
topics.desc: A positive whole-number exponent counts factors. Three to the fourth means 3 × 3 × 3 × 3, which is 81.

topics.title: Square roots
topics.desc: The principal square root of a nonnegative number is the nonnegative value whose square equals it. The square root of 49 is 7.

topics.title: Prime numbers
topics.desc: A prime is a whole number greater than one with exactly two positive divisors: one and itself. For 29, testing primes up to its square root is enough.

topics.title: Greatest common factor
topics.desc: List the factors both numbers share and select the largest. For 18 and 24, the greatest common factor is 6.

topics.title: Least common multiple
topics.desc: List positive multiples until one repeats across both lists. For 4 and 6 the first common positive multiple is 12.

topics.title: Simplifying fractions
topics.desc: Divide the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor. For example, 18/24 divided top and bottom by 6 becomes 3/4.

topics.title: Mixed numbers
topics.desc: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator and keep the denominator. Three and two fifths becomes 17/5.

topics.title: Median
topics.desc: Sort the data. Take the middle value for an odd count or average the middle two for an even count.

topics.title: Mode
topics.desc: Count how often each value appears. The highest frequency determines the mode; a tie can give multiple modes.

topics.title: Data range
topics.desc: Subtract the smallest observed value from the largest. For 4, 7 and 12, the range is 8.

topics.title: Triangle area
topics.desc: Use half the base times its perpendicular height. With base 8 cm and height 5 cm, the area is 20 square centimeters.

topics.title: Circle circumference
topics.desc: Circumference is pi times diameter, or twice pi times radius. A circle with diameter 10 cm has circumference about 31.4 cm.

topics.title: Box volume
topics.desc: Multiply inside length, width and height in matching units. A 2 by 3 by 4 cm box has 24 cubic centimeters of interior volume.

topics.title: Measuring angles
topics.desc: Place the center on the vertex and align one ray with zero. Read the scale starting at that zero where the other ray crosses.

topics.title: Reading a ruler
topics.desc: Count the equal spaces between two numbered marks. Ten spaces in one centimeter mark millimeters. Start measuring from the zero mark.

topics.title: Scale drawings
topics.desc: Multiply the drawing length by the real distance per drawing unit. At 1 cm to 5 m, a 4 cm line represents 20 m.

topics.title: Estimating an answer
topics.desc: Round the inputs to easy nearby values and repeat the operation. Compare the order of magnitude and sign with your original result.

topics.title: PS5 backward compatibility
topics.desc: Most PS4 games run on PS5. For a disc copy you need a PS5 with a compatible disc drive, and the disc generally stays inserted while playing. For digital purchases, sign in to the account that owns the game and check its library.

topics.title: Disc versus digital games
topics.desc: Both versions usually install game files to storage. For a disc purchase, the disc normally proves you own the game when you launch it. For a download, the license is tied to your account.

topics.title: Save files
topics.desc: The installed game and the save are separate. The save records things like checkpoints and settings. Before removing anything, check where the game stores progress and which account you used.

topics.title: Cloud saves
topics.desc: A cloud save is a copy of your progress stored online. To continue elsewhere, check the right account, game version and sync status. Check timestamps before replacing a newer save.

topics.title: Cross-play
topics.desc: Cross-play lets players on supported platforms play together. Both the game and the chosen mode must support it. Cross-progression, which carries your save between platforms, is a separate feature.

topics.title: Split-screen games
topics.desc: Split-screen divides one display into views for local players. Check whether the particular game and mode support local multiplayer; online multiplayer alone doesn't guarantee it.

topics.title: Input lag
topics.desc: Input lag is the time between a control action and the visible response. Try the display's game mode, test in an offline scene and change one setting at a time to separate display delay from network lag.

topics.title: Controller dead zone
topics.desc: The dead zone ignores small movements near a stick's center. Lowering it can make tiny inputs register sooner; raising it slightly can mask drift, at the cost of fine control.

topics.title: Stick drift
topics.desc: Stick drift means the controller reports movement even when the stick is centered. Test another game or a controller input screen. Compare a second controller if possible; a slightly larger dead zone can mask small drift.

topics.title: Field of view
topics.desc: Field of view controls how much of the scene you can see. A wider view shows more around you but makes distant targets look smaller on the same screen.

topics.title: Motion blur
topics.desc: Motion blur simulates smearing during fast movement. Toggle it in the same scene and turn the camera at the same speed to judge whether details are easier for you to follow.

topics.title: Game subtitles
topics.desc: Subtitles usually show dialogue. Closed captions can also identify sounds or speakers. Check the game's accessibility settings for the available options.

topics.title: Matchmaking
topics.desc: Matchmaking looks for available players that fit the mode's rules. Region, connection quality, party size, skill criteria and the number of people online can affect the wait.

topics.title: Patch notes
topics.desc: Patch notes summarize changes such as bug fixes, balance adjustments or new features. Check the version and platform so you read the changes that apply to your game.

topics.title: Minecraft crafting
topics.desc: A crafting table provides a three-by-three grid for recipes that don't fit in your inventory's two-by-two grid. Craft a table from four planks, place it and interact with it.

topics.title: Minecraft survival and creative
topics.desc: Survival involves gathering resources and managing threats. Creative gives access to a large block inventory and flight, which makes it useful for trying a design before building it in Survival.

topics.title: Keyboard switches
topics.desc: Linear switches move smoothly, tactile switches have a bump and clicky switches add an audible click. The keycaps and keyboard case affect the sound too.

topics.title: Mouse DPI
topics.desc: DPI describes how many movement counts a mouse reports per inch of travel. Higher DPI usually moves the pointer farther at the same software sensitivity.

topics.title: USB connectors
topics.desc: USB-C describes the connector shape. Cables and ports with that shape can support different charging power, data speeds and video features. Compare specifications for both ends.

topics.title: Solid-state drives
topics.desc: An SSD stores files on flash memory. It can fetch data without moving a mechanical head, which helps games and apps load. Loading speed also depends on the rest of the device.

topics.title: Operating systems
topics.desc: An operating system manages memory, files, devices and access for applications. iOS, Linux and Windows are examples.

topics.title: Web browsers
topics.desc: A browser retrieves page resources, interprets their structure and styling, and can run JavaScript to make the page interactive.

topics.title: Search engines
topics.desc: A search engine builds an index of pages and ranks matches to your search. Your browser is the app you use to visit the results.

topics.title: Download versus upload
topics.desc: Uploading sends data from your device, such as backing up a video. Downloading brings data to your device, such as installing a game.

topics.title: Airplane mode
topics.desc: Airplane mode turns off cellular communication. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth can often be enabled separately. A locally stored app can still work without internet.

topics.title: Screenshots
topics.desc: A screenshot saves a still image of the visible screen. Crop out unrelated details before sharing; use a recording when the order of actions matters.

topics.title: Screen recordings
topics.desc: A screen recording captures a sequence of actions as video. Start just before the bug, repeat it once and stop so someone can see the exact sequence.

topics.title: Cropping a photo
topics.desc: Cropping selects the part of the image you keep. Move the frame around the subject and check the final shape before exporting a copy.

topics.title: Aspect ratios
topics.desc: Aspect ratio is the width relative to height. A 16:9 clip on a differently shaped screen needs bars, cropping or stretching to fill the space.

topics.title: Image compression
topics.desc: Compression encodes an image more efficiently. Lossless compression preserves its data; lossy compression can discard fine details to cut the file size further.

topics.title: PNG versus JPEG
topics.desc: PNG is often useful for sharp graphics or transparency. JPEG often gives smaller photos, though heavy compression can create artifacts around edges.

topics.title: Transparent backgrounds
topics.desc: Transparent pixels let the layer underneath show through. Many editors use a checkerboard to preview transparency; export to a format that supports it, such as PNG.

topics.title: Vector graphics
topics.desc: Vector graphics describe paths and shapes mathematically. The renderer redraws them at the requested size rather than enlarging a fixed grid of pixels.

topics.title: Pixels
topics.desc: A pixel is a sample in a digital image grid. Enlarging a small image reveals the limited detail stored in that grid.

topics.title: Layers in an editor
topics.desc: Keep text, background and objects on separate layers. You can move or hide one element while preserving the others.

topics.title: Audio tracks
topics.desc: Separate audio tracks let you lower music during speech and adjust each part independently. Listen through the transition before exporting.

topics.title: Muting versus lowering volume
topics.desc: Mute silences a track while retaining its level setting. Lowering the level changes the balance you hear when the track plays.

topics.title: Trimming a clip
topics.desc: Drag the clip's start or end point inward on the timeline. Preview the cut; many editors let you extend it again while the source file remains available.

topics.title: Video timelines
topics.desc: The timeline arranges clips along time. Move a clip earlier or later, and use separate tracks for elements that should overlap.

topics.title: Undo and redo
topics.desc: Undo reverses the last supported edit. Redo reapplies an edit you undid; making a new edit can discard the redo chain.

topics.title: File paths
topics.desc: A path lists folders leading to a file. In school/science/report.txt, open school, then science, then report.txt.

topics.title: Folder hierarchies
topics.desc: Choose one top-level folder per project, then a few subfolders such as photos, drafts and final. Keep naming consistent so you can predict where a new file belongs.

topics.title: File backups
topics.desc: Keep a separate recoverable copy and test opening it. A backup with older versions can help if a bad change or deletion spreads to your current copy.

topics.title: Syncing files
topics.desc: Sync keeps selected files aligned across devices. Changes and deletions may propagate, so check the service's trash and version history before making more edits.

topics.title: Read-only access
topics.desc: Read-only access lets you view content while editing the original requires additional permission. Ask the owner for edit access if you need to change the shared version.

topics.title: QR codes
topics.desc: A QR code stores encoded information such as text or a URL. Read the address preview before opening a link.

topics.title: Browser tabs
topics.desc: A tab holds a page inside a browser window. Windows can each have their own set of tabs; close or group tabs by task to find the one you want.

topics.title: Bookmarks folders
topics.desc: Create bookmark folders by purpose, such as school or projects. Give similar pages distinct names and remove links you no longer use.

topics.title: Calendar reminders
topics.desc: Work backward from the event using travel and preparation time. Set the first reminder for when you must start getting ready.

topics.title: Notification organization
topics.desc: Separate time-sensitive alerts from updates you can check later. Adjust each app's notification categories where available.

topics.title: Introducing yourself
topics.desc: Say your name, mention what brought you there and ask one easy question about the shared activity.

topics.title: Starting a conversation
topics.desc: Start with something you both experienced, such as a class project. Ask an open question and leave space for their answer.

topics.title: Asking follow-up questions
topics.desc: Pick one detail they mentioned and ask about it. If they said they built a game, try “What part took the longest?”

topics.title: Taking turns in conversation
topics.desc: Wait for a pause, refer to the point you are answering and keep your contribution short enough for others to join.

topics.title: Clarifying a misunderstanding
topics.desc: Describe what you understood and ask if that was their meaning. A neutral question can clear things up before either person reacts.

topics.title: Disagreeing respectfully
topics.desc: Name the point you agree on first if there is one. Explain your different reasoning and ask how they reached theirs.

topics.title: Saying no to an invitation
topics.desc: Thank them for inviting you and give a clear answer. Suggest a different time only if you actually want to meet then.

topics.title: Thank-you notes
topics.desc: Mention the specific gift or favor and why you appreciated it. A short sincere detail usually means more than a long generic message.

topics.title: Borrowing something
topics.desc: Name the item, explain when you will return it and give the owner room to say no. Check before passing it to anyone else.

topics.title: Returning something borrowed
topics.desc: Give it back on time in the condition you received it. If it is damaged or late, tell the owner directly and discuss how to put things right.

topics.title: Introducing two friends
topics.desc: Say both names and offer one shared interest that can start a conversation. Let each person tell their own story.

topics.title: Welcoming a newcomer
topics.desc: Introduce yourself, show them where things are and invite them into one specific activity. Offer a partner for the first drill.

topics.title: Sharing credit
topics.desc: When showing the work, name what each person contributed. Give credit beside the relevant part so their role is clear.

topics.title: Offering help
topics.desc: Ask which part they want help with. Offer a hint or demonstrate one example, then let them try the next step.

topics.title: Asking for help
topics.desc: State the goal, what you tried and where the result differed from your expectation. Include one small example.

topics.title: Listening actively
topics.desc: Let them finish, then briefly restate your understanding. Ask whether you got it right before offering advice.

topics.title: Planning a meetup spot
topics.desc: Agree on one exact landmark, a time and a backup plan. “Inside the main entrance beside the map” is clearer than just “at the park.”

topics.title: RSVPs
topics.desc: RSVP asks you to tell the host whether you will attend. Reply by the requested date and mention the event so the host can track responses.

topics.title: Leaving a voicemail
topics.desc: Say who you are, why you called and what response you need. Repeat your callback details clearly if the person doesn't already have them.

topics.title: Writing a clear text
topics.desc: Put the main request first. Include a time or place if needed, and reread it once for anything that could have two meanings.

topics.title: Choosing a group activity
topics.desc: Narrow the options using real constraints such as time or distance, then vote or rotate who chooses.

topics.title: Taking meeting notes
topics.desc: Record decisions, assigned tasks, owners and deadlines. You rarely need every sentence people said.

topics.title: Setting an agenda
topics.desc: List the decisions you need and give each a time slot. Put unrelated ideas on a later list and end by confirming next steps.

topics.title: Giving directions
topics.desc: Start from a known location, give turns in order and include visible landmarks at confusing points. Mention the destination's entrance.

topics.title: Being a good spectator
topics.desc: Cheer effort and good play, follow the venue's rules and let the coaches give instructions. Treat officials and both teams respectfully.

topics.title: Sketching with shapes
topics.desc: Break the object into a few circles, boxes or cylinders. Adjust their relative sizes before drawing details.

topics.title: Contour drawing
topics.desc: A contour follows the visible edges and changes of shape. Look at the object frequently and draw slowly enough to notice small turns.

topics.title: Shading a sphere
topics.desc: Choose a light direction. Leave the light-facing area bright, shade progressively around the curve and add a cast shadow on the opposite side.

topics.title: One-point perspective
topics.desc: For one-point perspective, set a horizon line and one vanishing point. Parallel edges going directly away from you aim toward that point.

topics.title: Mixing paint colors
topics.desc: Start with a small amount of the lighter color. Add the stronger color a little at a time and test a swatch before mixing a large batch.

topics.title: Warm and cool colors
topics.desc: Reds, oranges and yellows often feel warm; blues and some greens feel cool. Nearby colors change how warm a particular shade appears.

topics.title: Complementary colors
topics.desc: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on a chosen color wheel. On a traditional artist's wheel, blue and orange are a pair.

topics.title: Negative space
topics.desc: Negative space is the area around and between objects. Sketching those shapes helps check proportions.

topics.title: Tracing versus freehand
topics.desc: Tracing follows an existing outline. Freehand drawing builds the shapes yourself using observation or imagination; each exercises a different skill.

topics.title: Keeping a sketchbook
topics.desc: Choose one nearby object and draw it from three angles. Date the page and note one detail you noticed on the second try.

topics.title: Paper collage
topics.desc: Lay out the largest shapes first, overlap smaller pieces and take a photo of the arrangement before gluing.

topics.title: Folding a paper airplane
topics.desc: Fold along a clear centerline and match wing edges and angles. Check the plane from the front for uneven bends.

topics.title: Origami creases
topics.desc: Align the corners before pressing. Hold them in place, then crease from the center outward on a flat surface.

topics.title: Lettering a title
topics.desc: Mark the midpoint of the space and sketch the word lightly with room for each letter. Adjust spacing before darkening it.

topics.title: Designing a logo
topics.desc: Sketch one simple silhouette based on the main idea. Shrink your sketch to icon size to check that it stays recognizable.

topics.title: Making a comic strip
topics.desc: Give each panel one visible moment or change. Thumbnail the sequence and leave space for dialogue before drawing the final art.

topics.title: Storyboarding
topics.desc: Draw rough frames in order. Under each, note the action, camera position and sound so you know what to capture.

topics.title: Character goals
topics.desc: Give the character a specific goal, a reason it matters and an obstacle that forces a choice. Show progress or a setback in each scene.

topics.title: Writing dialogue
topics.desc: Give each speaker a different priority and rhythm. Read the scene aloud and remove lines that only explain things both characters know.

topics.title: Describing a setting
topics.desc: Choose a few concrete details the character would notice, such as a sound or an object in use. Let the details affect what happens.

topics.title: Writing a haiku
topics.desc: Focus on one observed moment and a shift in what you notice. If your assignment requests a 5–7–5 syllable pattern, count and revise after drafting.

topics.title: Rhymes
topics.desc: Rhymes share ending sounds, especially from the stressed vowel onward. Listen to the words aloud rather than judging spelling alone.

topics.title: Melody
topics.desc: The melody is the sequence of pitches and rhythms heard as a tune. Try humming the main line while ignoring the backing instruments.

topics.title: Chords
topics.desc: A chord combines notes sounding together as harmony. A melody is a sequence of notes unfolding over time.

topics.title: Playlists
topics.desc: Decide the mood you want at the beginning and end. Put songs with related energy near each other and listen to each transition.

topics.title: Reading a compass rose
topics.desc: Find the compass rose or north arrow. Rotate the map to match your surroundings if that makes the route easier to follow.

topics.title: Map legends
topics.desc: The legend pairs each color, line or symbol with its meaning. Check it before assuming a dashed line is a road or trail.

topics.title: Contour lines on maps
topics.desc: Each contour connects points at the same elevation. Closely spaced contours usually indicate a steeper slope; read the interval to see the height difference.

topics.title: Latitude
topics.desc: Latitude gives angular distance north or south of the equator, from zero to ninety degrees. Lines of equal latitude run east–west.

topics.title: Longitude
topics.desc: Longitude gives angular distance east or west of the prime meridian. Together with latitude it locates a point on Earth.

topics.title: Time zones
topics.desc: Different regions use different standard clock times as Earth rotates. Check both places and the date when scheduling, because seasonal clock changes can differ.

topics.title: Continents
topics.desc: A continent is a major geographic land region. A country is a political territory; one continent can include many countries.

topics.title: Islands
topics.desc: An island is land surrounded by water on all sides. It can lie in an ocean, lake or river.

topics.title: Peninsulas
topics.desc: A peninsula has water on most sides while remaining connected to a larger landmass. On a map, look for the land connection.

topics.title: Archipelagos
topics.desc: An archipelago is a group or chain of islands. The islands can vary widely in size.

topics.title: Lakes versus ponds
topics.desc: Both are inland bodies of water. Lakes are often larger or deeper, but there is no single size cutoff used everywhere.

topics.title: River tributaries
topics.desc: A tributary is a stream or river that flows into another stream or river. Follow the direction of flow to identify which joins which.

topics.title: River deltas
topics.desc: A river slows as it enters a larger body of water and can deposit sediment. If it accumulates, the deposits build a delta.

topics.title: Watersheds
topics.desc: A watershed is the area draining toward a shared outlet. Ridges often separate water flowing to different streams.

topics.title: Tides
topics.desc: The Moon's gravity and, to a lesser extent, the Sun's produce tides. Coastline shape and local geography affect their timing and height.

topics.title: Ocean waves
topics.desc: Wind transfers energy to the water surface. Wave size depends on wind speed, how long it blows and how far it travels over open water.

topics.title: Sand dunes
topics.desc: Wind moves loose sand. When sand collects around an obstacle or the wind slows, a mound can grow; vegetation can help stabilize it.

topics.title: Erosion
topics.desc: Erosion moves sediment or rock away by water, wind, ice or gravity. Look for both a source of material and the place it collects.

topics.title: Weathering
topics.desc: Weathering breaks down or changes rock in place. Erosion carries the resulting material elsewhere.

topics.title: Cloud cover
topics.desc: Cloud cover describes how much of the visible sky is covered. Overcast means nearly or completely covered; cloud cover alone does not tell you whether rain will fall.

topics.title: Humidity
topics.desc: Relative humidity compares the vapor present to the amount air can sustain at its current temperature. Cooling air can raise relative humidity even without adding water.

topics.title: Wind direction
topics.desc: A north wind comes from the north and blows toward the south. Weather reports name winds by their origin.

topics.title: Rainbows
topics.desc: Sunlight bends as it enters droplets, reflects inside and bends again as it leaves. Different wavelengths bend by different amounts, separating the colors.

topics.title: Dew
topics.desc: Dew forms when a surface cools enough for nearby water vapor to condense on it. This often happens overnight as the ground loses heat.

topics.title: Frost
topics.desc: Frost can form when a surface is cold enough for water vapor to deposit as ice. A ground surface can be colder than the reported air temperature.

topics.title: Dribbling a soccer ball
topics.desc: Use small touches when space is tight and longer ones in open space. Practice changing direction around a marker while keeping the ball within a step.

topics.title: Soccer throw-ins
topics.desc: A throw-in goes to the opponents of the last player to touch the ball before it crossed the touchline. Face the field and use both hands from behind and over the head, with part of each foot on or outside the line.

topics.title: Corner kicks
topics.desc: When the whole ball crosses the goal line off a defender without a goal, the usual restart is a corner kick for the attacking team.

topics.title: Goal kicks
topics.desc: When the whole ball crosses the goal line off an attacker without a goal, the usual restart is a goal kick for the defending team.

topics.title: Soccer offside
topics.desc: Officials judge position when a teammate plays or touches the ball. In the opponents' half, being nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent can put you offside; interfering with play or an opponent matters too.

topics.title: Soccer formations
topics.desc: In a 4-3-3, the ten outfield players are grouped as four defenders, three midfielders and three forwards. The goalkeeper is counted separately.

topics.title: Soccer assists
topics.desc: An assist credits a player for helping set up a teammate's goal, often with the final pass. The exact statistical rule varies by competition.

topics.title: Soccer halftime
topics.desc: Halftime separates the two periods and gives teams a break and a chance to adjust tactics. They normally change ends for the second half.

topics.title: Basketball rebounds
topics.desc: A rebound is gaining possession after a missed shot. The shooting team's rebound is offensive; the opposing team's is defensive.

topics.title: Basketball traveling
topics.desc: Traveling is illegal foot movement while holding the ball. The call depends on gathering the ball, establishing a pivot foot and what the player does next.

topics.title: Basketball assists
topics.desc: A basketball assist is a pass judged to lead directly to a made basket. A long series of independent moves by the scorer can change the ruling.

topics.title: Basketball free throws
topics.desc: A free throw is an unguarded attempt from the free-throw line worth one point if made. The foul and game situation determine the number of attempts.

topics.title: Tennis scoring
topics.desc: In a standard game points go love, 15, 30, 40, then game. At 40–40, called deuce, a player normally needs two consecutive points to win.

topics.title: Tennis doubles
topics.desc: Doubles has two players per team and uses the wider doubles sidelines during rallies. The serve still lands in the diagonal service box.

topics.title: Volleyball rotation
topics.desc: In standard indoor volleyball, the receiving team rotates one position clockwise when it wins the right to serve. Winning another point while already serving doesn't trigger a rotation.

topics.title: Badminton rallies
topics.desc: A rally is the exchange starting with the serve and ending when the shuttle is out of play. Each side tries to land it in the opponent's court or force a fault.

topics.title: Relay races
topics.desc: Relay teammates cover separate legs in order. In baton events, the exchange must happen inside the designated zone.

topics.title: Personal bests
topics.desc: A personal best is your best recorded result for a particular event. Compare the same distance and conditions when interpreting progress.

topics.title: Tournament brackets
topics.desc: Read a bracket from the opening matches toward the final. In single elimination each loser exits and each winner advances along the connecting line.

topics.title: Round-robin tournaments
topics.desc: In a single round robin, every team meets every other team once. With six teams each plays five games, giving fifteen matches in total.

topics.title: Keeping score
topics.desc: Agree on the scoring rules first and record each point or scoring play as it happens. Confirm the running total at natural breaks.

topics.title: Practicing a weak foot
topics.desc: Start with short stationary passes against a target using the weaker foot. Increase distance or movement after the direction becomes consistent.

topics.title: Bicycle gears
topics.desc: A lower gear needs less force per pedal stroke but travels less distance per turn. Shift before a steep section when possible and ease pedal pressure during the change.

topics.title: Bicycle frame sizes
topics.desc: Wheel diameter describes the wheel. Frame dimensions and geometry affect reach and riding position. Check the maker's sizing chart and how the bike fits you.

topics.title: BMX pegs
topics.desc: Pegs are short extensions mounted near the axles on compatible BMX bikes. Their fit depends on axle size, hub hardware and intended use.

topics.title: Mirrors
topics.desc: A smooth mirror reflects rays in predictable directions. Your eyes trace the reflected rays back and perceive a virtual image behind the surface.

topics.title: Refraction
topics.desc: Light changes direction as it crosses between water and air at an angle. Your eyes interpret the submerged portion as coming from a different position.

topics.title: Magnifying glasses
topics.desc: A converging lens held close enough to the object produces an enlarged virtual image. Adjust its distance until the letters look sharp.

topics.title: Color filters
topics.desc: A colored filter transmits some wavelengths more strongly than others. Its effect also depends on which wavelengths are present in the incoming light.

topics.title: Pitch
topics.desc: Pitch mainly follows frequency. Faster vibrations produce a higher pitch; increasing volume alone does not raise the note.

topics.title: Loudness
topics.desc: Larger pressure variations generally sound louder. Distance from the source and the listener's sensitivity to different frequencies also matter.

topics.title: Vibrating strings
topics.desc: A plucked string vibrates. Its motion transfers energy to the guitar body or a pickup system, and the resulting air vibrations reach your ears.

topics.title: Static electricity
topics.desc: Rubbing can transfer electric charge to a balloon. That charge shifts nearby charges in the wall slightly, creating an attractive force.

topics.title: Magnets
topics.desc: Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Turn one magnet around to change which poles face each other.

topics.title: Gravity
topics.desc: Earth's gravity pulls objects toward its center. Close to the surface, objects in free fall accelerate at roughly the same rate if air resistance is small.

topics.title: Friction
topics.desc: Contact friction opposes sliding and transfers some mechanical energy into heat. A smoother or different surface can change how quickly the book slows.

topics.title: Inertia
topics.desc: Inertia is the tendency to keep the same velocity until a net force changes it. When a bus brakes, a passenger's body tends to continue forward.

topics.title: Levers
topics.desc: A lever pivots around a fulcrum. Applying force farther from the pivot increases its turning effect, trading a longer movement for less force.

topics.title: Pulleys
topics.desc: A fixed pulley redirects tension, so pulling downward can lift upward. With a moving pulley, multiple supporting rope segments can reduce the force needed.

topics.title: Gears
topics.desc: The teeth of two meshing external gears push each other, so they rotate in opposite directions. The gear with fewer teeth makes more turns.

topics.title: Insulation
topics.desc: Insulation slows heat transfer. Trapped air or a vacuum reduces some transfer paths, and a lid limits exchange with the surrounding air.

topics.title: Melting
topics.desc: Heat transferred into ice can let its molecules leave the ordered solid structure while remaining close together as liquid water.

topics.title: Freezing
topics.desc: As water freezes under ordinary conditions, molecules arrange into a more open structure. The resulting ice occupies more volume than the same mass of liquid water.

topics.title: Dissolving
topics.desc: Water molecules surround and disperse sugar molecules through the liquid. The sugar is still present, which is why the solution tastes sweet.

topics.title: Mixtures
topics.desc: A mixture contains multiple substances combined physically. Its proportions can vary, unlike a pure compound with a fixed chemical composition.

topics.title: Seed germination
topics.desc: Germination begins when suitable conditions let a seed resume growth. Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature are common requirements, and the root often emerges first.

topics.title: Plant roots
topics.desc: Roots anchor the plant and absorb water and dissolved minerals. Some also store food reserves.

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.desc: Plants use light energy to build sugars from carbon dioxide and water. The sugars supply material and energy for growth, and oxygen is released.

topics.title: Pollination
topics.desc: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to a flower's receptive structure. Animals, wind or other mechanisms can carry it; pollination can enable seed formation.

topics.title: Composting
topics.desc: Microorganisms break down suitable organic materials. A mix of moist scraps and dry leaves or paper, with air and some moisture, helps produce compost.

topics.title: Reading a bus schedule
topics.desc: Choose the route, direction and correct day. Follow one trip's column or row from your boarding stop to the destination, checking the table headings.

topics.title: Transfer stops
topics.desc: A transfer means leaving one vehicle and boarding another to finish the journey. Check the stop location, direction, wait time and applicable fare rules.

topics.title: Round-trip tickets
topics.desc: A one-way ticket covers travel in one direction. A round trip includes an outbound and return journey subject to the operator's route and date conditions.

topics.title: Packing for a day trip
topics.desc: Check the planned activity, weather and length of the outing. Pack what you will actually use and confirm tickets, directions and the return plan.

topics.title: Checking a forecast
topics.desc: Look at the hourly forecast for the place and hours you will be outside. Compare temperature, precipitation chance and wind instead of relying only on the day's high.

topics.title: Making an itinerary
topics.desc: Put fixed-time activities on the schedule first, group nearby stops and leave travel and waiting time. Decide which optional stop to skip if you run late.

topics.title: Finding a library book
topics.desc: Find the call number in the catalog and check its section or location. Match the shelf-end labels, then compare the letters and numbers in order.

topics.title: Library holds
topics.desc: A hold puts you in a queue or requests an available copy for pickup. Check the pickup location and wait for the ready notice before traveling.

topics.title: Renewing a library loan
topics.desc: Renewal extends a loan if the library allows it. Check the updated due date; another reader's hold or a renewal limit may prevent an extension.

topics.title: Comparing unit prices
topics.desc: Divide price by quantity in the same units for both packages. Compare the resulting price per ounce, item or other unit, then consider whether you will use the full package.

topics.title: Reading a receipt
topics.desc: Compare each item's quantity and price with what you bought. Then check discounts, applicable tax and the final payment total.

topics.title: Counting change
topics.desc: Count up from the price to the amount paid. From $13.65 to $14 is $0.35, then $6 to reach $20, so the change is $6.35.

topics.title: Measuring furniture
topics.desc: Measure width, depth and height of the desk, plus the space and the delivery path. Include door openings, tight turns, drawers and room to sit.

topics.title: Addressing an envelope
topics.desc: For a standard US envelope, put the recipient near the center, the return address at upper left and postage at upper right. Include the ZIP code.

topics.title: Postcards
topics.desc: Write the recipient's full mailing address in the address area, put your message beside it and apply the correct postage. Check destination and postal requirements.

topics.title: Reading a wall clock
topics.desc: The long hand gives minutes, five for each numbered step. The short hand indicates the hour it has passed; halfway from 3 to 4 with the minute hand on 6 means 3:30.

topics.title: Using a checklist
topics.desc: Write short action items in the order you actually do them. Try the checklist once and adjust anything that was vague, missing or unnecessary.

topics.title: Solving for x
topics.desc: Use inverse operations to isolate x. What you do to one side of the equation, do to the other. For 2x + 3 = 11, subtract 3 from both sides, then divide both sides by 2 to get x = 4.

topics.title: Slope of a line
topics.desc: Slope is the steepness of a line: rise over run, or the change in y divided by the change in x. A slope of 2/3 means the line goes up 2 units when it goes right 3 units. A negative slope goes down as it goes right.

topics.title: Linear equations
topics.desc: A linear equation graphs as a straight line. A common form is y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept, the point where the line crosses the y-axis.

topics.title: Inequalities
topics.desc: An inequality compares values with symbols such as <, >, ≤ or ≥. Solving one is like solving an equation, except that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.

topics.title: Systems of equations
topics.desc: A system is two or more equations considered together. A solution is a set of values that makes every equation true. You can solve by graphing, substitution, or elimination, which adds or subtracts equations to cancel a variable.

topics.title: The Pythagorean theorem
topics.desc: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle, and a and b are the other two sides. If the legs are 3 and 4, the hypotenuse is 5.

topics.title: Similar triangles
topics.desc: Similar triangles have the same shape but may differ in size. Their corresponding angles are equal, and corresponding sides are in the same ratio. You can use that ratio to find a missing side.

topics.title: Volume of a cylinder
topics.desc: The volume of a cylinder is πr²h, the area of the circular base times the height. Use the same units for the radius and the height, and the result is in cubic units.

topics.title: Volume of a sphere
topics.desc: The volume of a sphere is (4/3)πr³, where r is the radius, the distance from the center to any point on the surface. If you know the diameter, divide it by 2 first to get the radius.

topics.title: Percent change
topics.desc: Percent change is the difference divided by the original amount, then multiplied by 100. A price that goes from $40 to $50 rises by 10/40, which is a 25 percent increase. A decrease uses the same formula and comes out negative or is called a decrease.

topics.title: Proportions
topics.desc: A proportion says two ratios are equal, such as 2/3 = 4/6. To solve for a missing value, you can cross-multiply: if a/b = c/d, then a times d equals b times c.

topics.title: Speed, distance and time
topics.desc: Speed equals distance divided by time. Distance equals speed times time, and time equals distance divided by speed. Use matching units, such as miles and hours if the speed is in miles per hour.

topics.title: Graphing a line
topics.desc: Pick x-values, compute the matching y-values from the equation, and plot those points. For y = mx + b, start at the y-intercept, then use the slope to find another point: rise the numerator and run the denominator.

topics.title: The distributive property
topics.desc: The distributive property says a(b + c) = ab + ac. Multiply the factor outside the parentheses by each term inside, and keep each term's sign. For example, 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12.

topics.title: Combining like terms
topics.desc: Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power, such as 3x and 5x. Add or subtract their coefficients and keep the variable part: 3x + 5x = 8x. Constants combine with constants, and 3x and 3x² are not like terms.

topics.title: Scientific notation
topics.desc: Scientific notation writes a number as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10. 5,400 is 5.4 × 10³, and 0.0032 is 3.2 × 10⁻³. A positive exponent means a larger number; a negative exponent means a fraction less than 1.

topics.title: Independent events
topics.desc: Two events are independent if one outcome does not change the probability of the other, such as two flips of a fair coin. For independent events, multiply their probabilities: the chance of heads then heads is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

topics.title: The scientific method
topics.desc: The scientific method is a way to test ideas: ask a question, form a hypothesis, plan a fair test, collect data, and draw a conclusion. Other people should be able to repeat the test to see if they get similar results.

topics.title: Hypotheses and theories
topics.desc: A hypothesis is a testable possible explanation for something you observed. A scientific theory is a well-supported explanation built from many tested hypotheses and a large body of evidence, not a guess. Theories can still be revised if new evidence appears.

topics.title: Atoms
