topics.desc: An atom is the basic unit of a chemical element. It has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around the nucleus. The number of protons, called the atomic number, identifies the element.

topics.title: Molecules
topics.desc: A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together. The atoms can be the same, as in O₂, or different, as in water, H₂O. The chemical formula tells you which atoms are in the molecule and how many of each.

topics.title: The periodic table
topics.desc: The periodic table organizes elements by atomic number. Rows are called periods and columns are called groups. Elements in the same group often have similar chemical properties, such as the noble gases in the far-right column.

topics.title: States of matter
topics.desc: The common states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. In a solid, particles are packed in a fixed shape. In a liquid they flow and take the shape of the container. In a gas they spread out to fill the available space. Heat or pressure can change the state.

topics.title: Density
topics.desc: Density is mass divided by volume. A material with higher density has more mass in the same amount of space. That is why a steel bolt sinks in water while a larger piece of wood can float: steel’s density is greater than water’s, and most wood is less dense than water.

topics.title: Acids and bases
topics.desc: Acids and bases are opposite kinds of substances in water. Acids increase hydrogen ion concentration and often taste sour, such as lemon juice. Bases decrease that concentration or increase hydroxide, and many feel slippery, such as soap. They can neutralize each other.

topics.title: pH
topics.desc: pH is a scale that usually runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or basic a water solution is. 7 is neutral, like pure water. Numbers below 7 are acidic and numbers above 7 are basic. Each step of 1 is a tenfold change in acidity.

topics.title: Chemical versus physical change
topics.desc: A physical change alters form but not the substance itself, such as melting ice or tearing paper. A chemical change makes a new substance, such as burning wood or baking a cake. Clues can include a new color, gas, temperature change or unexpected solid, though those clues are not proof by themselves.

topics.title: Animal and plant cells
topics.desc: Both animal and plant cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane. Plant cells also have a cell wall and usually chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and they often have a large central vacuole. Animal cells do not have a cell wall or chloroplasts.

topics.title: DNA
topics.desc: DNA is the molecule in cells that carries genetic instructions. It is shaped like a double helix, a twisted ladder, with paired bases: A with T, and C with G. Those instructions help determine how an organism grows and how its cells work.

topics.title: Food chains
topics.desc: A food chain shows how energy moves from one living thing to another. It often starts with a producer, such as a plant, that makes its own food. A consumer eats plants or other animals, and a decomposer breaks down dead material. Arrows point toward the eater, the direction energy flows.

topics.title: Ecosystems
topics.desc: An ecosystem is a community of living things plus the nonliving parts of their environment, such as water, soil, air and climate. A change in one part, like a drought or the loss of a species, can affect many other parts.

topics.title: The water cycle
topics.desc: The water cycle is the movement of water between Earth’s surface and the atmosphere. Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, and falls as precipitation. It can then flow as runoff, soak into the ground, or evaporate again.

topics.title: The solar system
topics.desc: The solar system is the Sun and everything that orbits it, including eight planets, moons, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets are rocky. The four outer planets are much larger and are mostly gas and ice. Gravity from the Sun keeps the planets in orbit.

topics.title: Solar and lunar eclipses
topics.desc: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and the Moon’s shadow falls on Earth. A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon and Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon. They do not occur every month because the Moon’s orbit is tilted.

topics.title: Plate tectonics
topics.desc: Earth’s outer shell is broken into large plates that move slowly over the mantle. Where plates meet they can pull apart, collide, or slide past each other. That movement helps explain earthquakes, many volcanoes, and the building of mountain ranges.

topics.title: Earthquakes
topics.desc: An earthquake is the shaking caused when rocks along a fault suddenly slip and release energy as seismic waves. Most earthquakes occur near tectonic plate boundaries. During shaking, drop to the ground, take cover under sturdy furniture, and hold on until it stops.

topics.title: Volcanoes
topics.desc: A volcano is an opening where molten rock, ash and gas can reach the surface. Most volcanoes form near plate boundaries, especially where a plate sinks or where plates pull apart. Magma is molten rock underground; once it reaches the surface it is called lava.

topics.title: Fossils
topics.desc: Fossils are remains or traces of past life, such as bones, shells, footprints or leaf impressions, preserved in rock. They form more often when an organism is buried quickly and hard parts are slowly replaced or left as an imprint. Fossils help scientists learn how life and environments have changed.

topics.title: Acceleration
topics.desc: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. An object accelerates if it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. In everyday use people often say acceleration only for speeding up, but in physics all of those changes count.

topics.title: Kinetic and potential energy
topics.desc: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Potential energy is stored energy because of position or condition, such as a bike at the top of a hill or a stretched spring. Energy can change from one form to the other, like a ball slowing as it rolls uphill and speeding up as it comes down.

topics.title: Simple circuits
topics.desc: A simple electric circuit is a closed loop that lets current flow from a power source through a load, such as a bulb, and back again. If the loop is broken, the current stops. A switch opens or closes the loop, and wires need a complete path of conductive material.

topics.title: Electrical conductors
topics.desc: An electrical conductor lets electric current flow easily. Metals such as copper and aluminum are common conductors and are used in wires. An electrical insulator, such as rubber, glass or many plastics, resists current and is used to coat wires for safety.

topics.title: The greenhouse effect
topics.desc: The greenhouse effect is the way some gases in the atmosphere, including carbon dioxide and water vapor, absorb heat and keep Earth warmer than it would be without them. A stronger greenhouse effect from extra greenhouse gases traps more heat and raises global average temperatures.

topics.title: Renewable energy
topics.desc: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished, such as sunlight, wind, moving water and geothermal heat. Fossil fuels like coal, oil and natural gas form much more slowly than we use them. Renewable sources still have costs, land use and other tradeoffs, but they do not run out in the same way.

topics.title: Recycling
topics.desc: Recycling turns used materials into new products instead of throwing them away. Rinse containers, follow your local rules, and keep items loose rather than bagged unless your collector says otherwise. Not everything with a recycling symbol is accepted curbside, so check the local list.

topics.title: The atmosphere
topics.desc: Earth’s atmosphere is the layer of gases around the planet. It is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with smaller amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. It provides air to breathe, helps protect the surface from much of the Sun’s harmful radiation, and is where weather happens.

topics.title: Microscopes
topics.desc: A microscope magnifies things that are too small to see clearly with your eyes alone. A compound light microscope uses lenses and light; start on the lowest power, use the coarse knob to find the specimen, then sharpen with the fine knob. Keep slides thin and never use the coarse knob on high power.

topics.title: The human heart
topics.desc: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood through the body. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body. Valves keep blood moving in one direction.

topics.title: The lungs
topics.desc: The lungs are where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it. When you inhale, air travels down the windpipe to smaller airways and into tiny air sacs called alveoli. Oxygen crosses into the blood there, and carbon dioxide crosses out to be exhaled.

topics.title: Digestion
topics.desc: Digestion breaks food into nutrients the body can absorb. It starts in the mouth with chewing and saliva, continues in the stomach, and most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine. The large intestine absorbs water and forms leftover material into stool.
